title: What is HTML?
summary: Explains the role of HTML among the three front-end file types, then unpacks the name Hypertext Markup Language: hypertext means linked documents, markup means tags that label parts of the content. Sets up the heading tag as the first element to learn.

concepts.heading: Where HTML fits in a website
points: Every browser (Chrome, Safari, Brave, etc.) does the same job: it reads HTML, CSS and JavaScript files and renders them as a web page.
Modern sites combine all three, but only HTML can stand on its own. A CSS file alone or a JavaScript file alone does not make a page; an HTML file alone does.
The earliest websites were nothing but HTML.
HTML's job is the content and structure of the page. Example: a file containing just a heading element reading 'My Website' opens in the browser as that heading and nothing else.
(Extra) Rough division of labour used for the rest of the course: HTML = structure/content, CSS = appearance, JavaScript = behaviour.

concepts.heading: Hypertext
points: Hypertext is text that links to another document. Links (hyperlinks) are the core mechanism the whole web of HTML pages is built on.

The first website, built by Tim Berners-Lee, is mostly blue hyperlinks. Clicking one (e.g. from Project.html) loads a different HTML file. Navigating a site is just moving between linked HTML documents.
(Extra) Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web (HTML, HTTP, URLs) rather than the Internet itself, which is the underlying network. The first site is still online at info.cern.ch.

concepts.heading: Markup language
points: Markup means adding symbols around content to say what that content is, rather than adding content itself. Quotation marks in English are a familiar example: they tell the reader a passage is a quote.
Another comparison is an editor annotating a manuscript with marks for bold, underline and so on.
HTML does its markup with tags: keywords inside angle brackets, wrapped around the content they label.
Early HTML had only a few tags. Today there are many, but day-to-day work uses a small core set, such as headings h1 to h6 and the paragraph tag p.
No need to memorise the full tag list. The course introduces each tag when a project or exercise needs it, and MDN's element reference lists the rest.

code_examples.caption: (Extra) The smallest useful HTML file: one heading, which the browser renders on its own with no CSS or JS
(Extra) Markup in practice: tags label what each piece of text is; the a tag is the hypertext part
code_examples.code:
My Website

This is a paragraph of text.

About me

pitfalls: Thinking a site can be built from CSS or JavaScript alone: there must always be an HTML document for them to attach to.
Trying to learn every HTML tag up front instead of learning them as they come up.
(Extra) Confusing the Web (documents linked by hypertext) with the Internet (the network it runs on).

gaps_and_ideas: Add a short intro lesson (e.g. id 's02-what-is-html', lesson '2.0') with blurb: 'HTML is the one file a website cannot do without. Hypertext = linked documents; markup = tags that label content.'

Tasks: (1) open a blank file and type

My Website

, see it render with no CSS/JS; (2) wrap a sentence in

and compare it to the unwrapped text; (3) add an link to a second page and click it to see hypertext in action; (4) list three tags you already recognise.
Starter code idea: an empty body with a TODO comment plus a second tiny page (page2.html) to link to, so the hyperlink task actually navigates.

Interactive demo idea: a three-toggle 'layer switcher' (HTML only / + CSS / + JS) on the same mini page so learners see that turning off CSS and JS still leaves readable content, but turning off HTML leaves nothing.
Second demo idea: a 'markup highlighter' that shows plain text on one side and the tagged version on the other, with each tag coloured, mirroring the quotation-marks analogy.
